# Why am I not moving after starting car and shifting to Drive?

When you start an automatic transmission vehicle and shift into Drive, the engine should immediately engage the torque converter to propel the vehicle. If your car idles high upon startup—around 1500 RPM—and refuses to move until those RPMs drop below 1000 after several minutes of warming up, the issue is almost certainly hydraulic rather than mechanical in terms of broken gears. The fact that Reverse works immediately confirms that the transmission control module (TCM) and main powertrain are functional; the problem is isolated to how pressure builds or holds within the specific circuits for forward gears.

The high initial idle you observe is a deliberate design feature known as fast idle. Modern Engine Control Units (ECUs) command a higher RPM during cold starts to ensure the engine reaches operating temperature quickly and to prevent stalling due to thickened oil viscosity. However, this behavior reveals a secondary issue: the transmission fluid is not building sufficient line pressure immediately upon startup. In an automatic transmission, hydraulic pressure is required to push pistons into clutch packs or apply bands that lock specific gear sets together. If the pump isn't generating enough flow or if there's a restriction in the filter, the clutches slip until the engine speed increases enough to overcome the resistance.

The symptom where the car only moves once RPMs drop below 1000 is the critical diagnostic clue. As the engine warms up naturally from that initial 1500 RPM idle, the transmission fluid expands and becomes less viscous (thinner). Thinner oil allows the pump to generate higher pressure with less internal friction, eventually crossing the threshold needed to fully engage the forward clutches. This explains why revving the engine to 4000 RPM speeds up the process; you are artificially increasing the flow rate through the transmission cooler and filter, bypassing the restriction that is slowing down pressure buildup at idle speed.

A common point of failure in this scenario is a clogged or partially blocked transmission filter. Over time, clutch material breaks down into particulates that accumulate behind the filter element. When the fluid first starts flowing after a cold start, it must pass through this debris-clogged section to reach the pressure regulator and valve body. The restriction causes a delay in pressure buildup at low RPMs but resolves as fluid temperature lowers viscosity or engine speed forces more flow. Conversely, if the issue were worn pump gears or a leaking seal, the problem would persist regardless of RPM because there wouldn't be enough mechanical displacement to generate pressure even at 4000 RPM.

Another possibility involves the transmission cooler lines or the radiator cooler itself. If debris has accumulated in the external cooling circuit, it can restrict flow when the system is cold and contracted. As the metal expands with heat, the restriction might open slightly, allowing adequate pressure to develop. However, this is less common than an internal filter issue given the specific RPM dependency described.

To confirm these hypotheses without a full teardown, you would need a transmission pressure gauge connected to the test port on the valve body. Monitoring line pressure while holding the throttle at different cold-start RPMs will show if pressure eventually reaches specification or if it caps out low, indicating pump wear versus flow restriction. If the pressure builds correctly once warm but takes too long, the filter is the primary suspect and should be replaced along with a fluid flush to remove accumulated varnish and metal shavings.
